debates.motion: Does the Kalam cosmological argument show that the universe began to exist, has a cause, and points to a personal creator?

routes.description: The defender’s route applies the causal principle to a universe whose finite temporal beginning is established by arguments against an actual infinite and against formation by successive addition, then identifies a personal agent as the best explanation of the universe’s first effect.
routes.successCriteria: Establish that the past is finite, that the universe consequently began and has a cause, and that an eternal impersonal mechanism cannot explain a temporally first universe whereas personal agency can.

bridges.description: The Kalam shows that the universe began to exist, has a cause, and points to a personal creator.
A beginningless past would contain an actually infinite number of events; because such an actual infinite cannot exist, the temporal series and universe began.
Hilbert-style concrete scenarios reveal that an actually infinite collection is metaphysically impossible, despite the consistency of infinite set theory.
An actually infinite temporal series cannot be formed by successive addition or completed by counting down from a beginningless past.
An eternal impersonal cause would produce its effect eternally or not at all, while a personal agent can freely originate a temporally first universe.

routes.description: The critic’s route argues that the Kalam does not exclude a beginningless material reality and that its paradoxes and conceptual analysis leave coherent infinite-past and impersonal-cause alternatives available.
routes.successCriteria: Show that actual-infinite scenarios establish strangeness rather than impossibility, that successive-addition reasoning does not rule out a beginningless series ending in the present, or that an impersonal indeterministic cause can explain a first universe without a personal creator.

bridges.description: The Kalam does not show that the universe began to exist, has a cause, and points to a personal creator.
The Kalam’s finitude and personhood inferences fail to exclude coherent beginningless-past or impersonal-origin alternatives, so its conclusion is not established.
The unusual behavior of Hilbert’s Hotel does not entail that an actually infinite collection is metaphysically impossible.
The impossibility of reaching the end of an endless count does not establish the impossibility of reaching the present end of a beginningless countdown.
An impersonal indeterministic cause could originate the universe at one time, so a personal cause is not uniquely required.

bridgeCoverage.description: The Kalam shows that the universe began to exist, has a cause, and points to a personal creator.
A beginningless past would contain an actually infinite number of events; because such an actual infinite cannot exist, the temporal series and universe began.
Hilbert-style concrete scenarios reveal that an actually infinite collection is metaphysically impossible, despite the consistency of infinite set theory.
An actually infinite temporal series cannot be formed by successive addition or completed by counting down from a beginningless past.
An eternal impersonal cause would produce its effect eternally or not at all, while a personal agent can freely originate a temporally first universe.
The Kalam does not show that the universe began to exist, has a cause, and points to a personal creator.
The Kalam’s finitude and personhood inferences fail to exclude coherent beginningless-past or impersonal-origin alternatives, so its conclusion is not established.
The unusual behavior of Hilbert’s Hotel does not entail that an actually infinite collection is metaphysically impossible.

bridgeCoverage.description: Given the available reason and evidence, belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God is irrational.

Apparently gratuitous evil and related epistemic confusion outweigh the proposed arguments for God and prevent those arguments from rationally supporting the all-powerful, all-loving God under discussion.
Pervasive suffering that appears to serve no greater good is improbable under an all-powerful, all-loving God, and merely possible theodicies do not make belief in that God rational.
An all-loving God would not attach grave eternal consequences to salvation conditions that sincere people cannot reliably identify and religious communities cannot agree upon.

Evolutionary accounts of cognition and morality, together with alternative explanations of apparent design, undercut the claim that reason, fine-tuning, or moral experience rationally identifies the proposed God.
The cumulative available evidence makes belief in God more rational than nonbelief.

The combined evidence from rational minds, cosmic design, and objective morality makes God more probable than God's nonexistence, while available responses prevent suffering from defeating that inference.
Unguided naturalism undermines confidence that evolved minds track truth, whereas an intelligent creator provides a rational basis for trusting human reason and the universe's intelligibility.
The universe's highly specific life-permitting conditions are substantially more probable under intelligent design than under an unguided chance hypothesis.
Objective moral obligations are difficult to ground in an impersonal, purposeless universe but are intelligible when goodness is grounded in God.

routes.description: A cumulative Christian-theist route arguing that cosmological origins, fine-tuning, objective morality, Jesus' resurrection, and personal religious experience jointly favor the Christian God over skeptical atheism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the cited evidence is established, its principal naturalistic alternatives are inadequate, and its combined explanatory force makes the specifically Christian God more reasonable than skeptical atheism.

bridges.description: The evidence from cosmology, fine-tuning, morality, Jesus' resurrection, and religious experience makes Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism.
The cumulative convergence of the five evidential lines supplies good reason to accept Christian theism and no comparably good reason to accept atheism.
The universe's finite beginning and need for a cause imply an uncaused, timeless, spaceless, immaterial transcendent cause.
The universe's life-permitting fine-tuning is better explained by intelligent design than by physical necessity or chance.
The empty tomb, post-mortem appearances, and origin of the disciples' resurrection belief are best explained by God raising Jesus from the dead.

routes.description: A skeptical-atheist route arguing that the proposed evidence is uncertain, underdetermines the Christian God, admits natural alternatives, and conflicts with what would be expected from an omnipotent, omniscient, morally perfect being.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the principal theistic inferences lack adequate evidential support or specificity and the observed world is at least as expected under skeptical atheism as under the Christian God hypothesis.

bridges.description: The cited evidence does not make Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism and instead supports withholding or rejecting belief in the Christian God.
The five proposed evidential lines fail to meet the strong burden required for the specific Christian God hypothesis because their inferences are underdetermined and face contrary empirical evidence.
The Kalam inference is inadequately supported because ordinary causal experience does not establish causation for creation ex nihilo or for the physical universe as a whole.
Fine-tuning probabilities are epistemically uncertain, admit deeper physical or multiverse explanations, and do not identify an omniperfect Christian God.
The world's evil and opaque divine presence are empirically less expected from a morally perfect Christian God than from skeptical atheism.

bridgeCoverage.description: The evidence from cosmology, fine-tuning, morality, Jesus' resurrection, and religious experience makes Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism.
The cumulative convergence of the five evidential lines supplies good reason to accept Christian theism and no comparably good reason to accept atheism.
The universe's finite beginning and need for a cause imply an uncaused, timeless, spaceless, immaterial transcendent cause.
The universe's life-permitting fine-tuning is better explained by intelligent design than by physical necessity or chance.
The empty tomb, post-mortem appearances, and origin of the disciples' resurrection belief are best explained by God raising Jesus from the dead.
The cited evidence does not make Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism and instead supports withholding or rejecting belief in the Christian God.
The five proposed evidential lines fail to meet the strong burden required for the specific Christian God hypothesis because their inferences are underdetermined and face contrary empirical evidence.
The Kalam inference is inadequately supported because ordinary causal experience does not establish causation for creation ex nihilo or for the physical universe as a whole.
Fine-tuning probabilities are epistemically uncertain, admit deeper physical or multiverse explanations, and do not identify an omniperfect Christian God.
The world's evil and opaque divine presence are empirically less expected from a morally perfect Christian God than from skeptical atheism.
